name: li-Duma
confidence_why: Puech 1990, a first-hand instrumental study of li-Duma, places stress on the first vowel of the stem, and the only other description, Reeb's 1895 missionary sketch, states a penult-or-antepenult counting rule that picks out that same stem-initial syllable in the ordinary prefix-plus-stem nouns, so the sources are few but the stem-initial reading has no serious rival.

Essai de grammaire douma (Haut-Ogowe, Congo francais). Mission Catholique, Libreville/Lastourville; printed B. Herder, Fribourg-en-Brisgau. 52 pp.]
catalog_locator: Puech 1990 sec. 4 'Phonetic evidence', pp. 180-181 (held 2-up scan page 4 of 7, read; retyped); li-Duma nominal forms p. 175 = scan page 1. Reeb 1895 ch. I 'De l'Alphabet' principle 8, p. 2 (p. 10, header '- 2 -').
catalog_quote: First, it may be noticed that in B50 Bantu (and more generally in West Bantu languages), the radical vowel (i.e. the first vowel of the stem) is stressed. The seven vowel system (a, ɛ, ɔ, e, o, i, u) obtains for this position only, and in some languages of the group, although not in li-Duma or li-Wanji, the final vowel is reduced or even dropped in connected speech and in isolation. Relative length is also a relevant cue to stress placement. In Figure 2 (a), compare for example prefixal [u] in the initial syllable and radical [u] in the stem -lumi: the latter is longer by approximately one half (106 vs 70 ms). ... We notice an overall increase in the total duration of insistent forms, primarily on the initial syllable and secondarily on the final one, whereas the radical stressed syllable is less affected. [Puech 1990: 180-181] ... L'accent, plus ou moins fort, suivant l'expression donnée au discours, se trouve pour les mots de deux et trois syllabes sur la pénultième; pour les mots de plus de trois syllabes il est placé sur l'antépénultième. [Reeb 1895: 2]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: rendered the 2-up scan we hold (7 A4 landscape pages, no text) and read scan page 4 (= printed pp. 180-181, sec. 4 'Phonetic evidence'). The reported passage is there verbatim, from 'First, it may be noticed that in B50 Bantu (and more generally in West Bantu languages), the radical vowel (i.e. the first vowel of the stem) is stressed' through '(106 vs 70 ms)'; the scan shows the IPA letters (a, ɛ, ɔ, e, o, i, u) exactly as the report quotes them (the retyped Pholia_N-5 text file renders them as E/O, so the report followed the scan, correctly). Page 181 also confirms the follow-up sentences used in rule_in_words: 'overall increase in the total duration of insistent forms, prima…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Duma is a two-tone language (H/L, with High-tone copying, downstep and a semantically conditioned upstep). Word stress is on the radical (stem-initial) vowel, i.e. the first vowel after the noun-class or verbal prefix; it is cued by duration and by the fact that the full seven-vowel contrast is restricted to that position. Under emphasis (the 'insistent' upstep forms) duration increases on the initial (prefix) and final syllables rather than on the stressed radical.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The older Duma-specific grammar (Reeb 1895, p. 2) gives a syllable-counting formulation instead: stress on the penult in words of two and three syllables and on the antepenult in longer words, stronger or weaker 'suivant l'expression donnée au discours'; for the canonical prefix + CVCV or prefix + CVCVCV word this coincides with the stem-initial syllable, but the two formulations differ for other shapes.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: nominal forms (prefix + stem) in isolation and in the presentative construction; the group-level wording ('in B50 Bantu') is made in a paper whose data are li-Duma (Lastoursville) and li-Wanji, and the duration example is a li-Wanji token, so the Duma application is by the author's inclusion of li-Duma in the claim, not a Duma-specific measurement.
new_statements.identity_note: Puech 1990 describes 'li-Duma' spoken around Lastoursville (= Duma proper, duma1253) alongside 'li-Wanji' (= Wandji/Liwanzi, wand1266, Guthrie B501), which he treats as two dialects of one language; the stress sentence is phrased for B50 Bantu as a group, and the duration measurement is on a li-Wanji token. Reeb 1895 describes 'douma' of the Haut-Ogowé mission at Lastourville, i.e. the same variety.

readall_conflicts: The only listed work could not be opened, so no new statement. 180-181, retyped the text) says that in B50 Bantu, li-Duma included, "the radical vowel (i.e. the first vowel of the stem) is stressed", with vowel-inventory restriction and length as cues, i.e. a morphologically anchored (root-initial) stress; Reeb 1895 (p. 2, principle 8, lines 155-158) says "L'accent.. se trouve pour les mots de deux et trois syllabes sur la pénultième; pour les mots de plus de trois syllabes il est placé sur l'antépénultième", i.e. a syllable-counting rule. The two coincide for the commonest prefix+CVCV nouns (mu-lu-mi: stem-initial = penult) but diverge for longer words (Reeb: antepenult; Puech: stem-initial wherever it falls). Reeb is a 1895 missionary sketch with no tone marking; Puech is an instrumental study by a phonologist and is the statement the catalog already carries.
